content: Good afternoon. I need to talk through some staffing issues that have come up this week — it's been a rough few days honestly. We're only into our second week of operation and I'm already dealing with more personnel problems than I expected. I want to lay everything out and think through the next steps carefully, because I can feel the pressure building and I don't want to make reactive decisions I'll regret later.

Good afternoon, Morishita-san. I'm glad you're taking the time to work through this methodically rather than just reacting — staffing problems in the first two weeks of operation are genuinely common, but that doesn't make them easy to manage, especially when you're simultaneously trying to establish service rhythms, calibrate your menu pacing, and build the early culture of the restaurant. The decisions you make right now about how to respond to personnel gaps tend to set patterns that carry forward, so the care you're bringing to this conversation is well placed. I also want to say: the fact that you're framing it as not wanting to make reactive decisions is important. Under pressure, restaurant operators often reach for the nearest available solution — hiring someone quickly without proper vetting, pulling a manager into floor coverage as a permanent workaround, or making promises to staff that create downstream complications. The better path is always to slow down slightly, understand what you actually need, and then move decisively once the picture is clear. That is what we will try to do here. Let me hear the full picture. What happened, and who is involved? Start from the beginning so I understand the scope before we move into problem-solving.

There are two separate issues happening at the same time, which is what makes it feel so overwhelming. The first — and most immediate — is that Naoki Hirose quit after 2 weeks. He came to me on Monday and told me he had been offered a higher-paying job at a hotel banquet operation in Shiodome and he was going to take it. He gave me two days' notice, which is technically something, but in practical terms it meant he was gone by Wednesday and I went into Thursday's service without him. The second issue is that sous chef Nakajima reports back pain and is reducing hours temporarily. He told me and Marco about it on Tuesday morning — so it hit the same week as Naoki. I'm short one server on the floor and running with a limited sous chef simultaneously, and I have full bookings through the weekend.

That is a significant double hit, especially this early in the life of the restaurant. I want to make sure I understand the impact of each situation clearly before we talk about responses, because the nature of the gap matters as much as the gap itself — and because the two problems interact with each other in ways that may not be obvious when you are in the middle of managing both of them simultaneously. On Naoki Hirose: he was one of your part-time servers working alongside Yui Tachibana, with Eiko Sawada managing the room overall. With him gone, you're now running Eiko as service manager and Yui as your only remaining part-time floor staff. Before we get to solutions, I want to understand the operational impact precisely. How many covers are you currently booking per service — and when Naoki was still with you, how was the floor coverage organized between the three of them? Were there specific sections or table assignments, or was it more fluid? I want to understand whether his departure leaves you at a level where service quality is genuinely at risk, or whether it's tight but manageable with some adjustment in how Eiko and Yui divide the room. On Nakajima: when he says he is reducing hours temporarily, what does that mean in concrete terms — is he coming in for shorter shifts, avoiding specific physical tasks, or only available on certain days of the week? And how did Marco respond when the three of you discussed it? His reaction will tell me a great deal about how serious the kitchen-side constraint actually is.

On floor staffing: we're booking between 22 and 28 covers per service right now. When Naoki was here, the plan was Eiko running the room as coordinator and managing guest relations, and Naoki and Yui splitting the tables between them. The first week had some rough spots — wine pour timing was a little uneven on one busy night, a couple of tables waited a bit longer than I would have liked — but nothing that alarmed me overall. Now, with just Yui and Eiko, it's tight. Eiko can run tables if she needs to, but she's strongest as a room coordinator and guest-facing manager, not as a plate carrier. If she's in the weeds on every table herself, nobody's watching the room as a whole and I lose the overview function she provides. On Nakajima: he is coming in, but he needs to avoid heavy lifting. No carrying large stockpots, no extended bending at the lower stations. He thinks two to three weeks and he should be back to full capacity. Marco's reaction was calm — he said he'd redistribute the mise en place tasks and restructure prep so Nakajima isn't doing the physical work that aggravates it. But Marco was also clear that if we push covers higher or add a special menu in the next two weeks, he'll need more hands in the kitchen.

Thank you — that gives me a clear picture, and I want to give you my honest read on each piece before we move into what to do about them. On the floor: 22 to 28 covers with Eiko and Yui is workable under normal circumstances, but it is fragile and the fragility compounds over consecutive services rather than being a problem you feel on any single night. Your instinct about Eiko is exactly right and I would reinforce it. The moment she is actively running tables herself, you lose the room-level visibility that is one of the most important functions a service manager provides. You stop catching the table that has been waiting six minutes for a wine top-up, or the guest who looks uncertain about a dish and would respond to a moment of attention, or the table that got their secondi before the couple at the next table who ordered first. Eiko's most valuable contribution to Osteria Morishita is not as a plate carrier — it is as the person who can see the room as a whole and make real-time adjustments that no one else is positioned to make. If she is buried in individual tables, that function disappears entirely. The risk is not any single service collapsing — it is that across multiple consecutive nights, both Eiko and Yui are working at the edge of their capacity, fatigue accumulates, small errors compound, and the experience you are trying to deliver starts to slip in ways that are genuinely hard to attribute to any single moment or decision. Guests do not go home and say the service was short-staffed. They go home and say it felt a little rushed, or they felt slightly neglected, or the energy in the room was off. You need a replacement for Naoki Hirose sooner than comfort would suggest. On Nakajima: Marco's composure is a meaningful signal and I do not want you to dismiss it. When a head chef responds to a personnel constraint with calm task redistribution rather than alarm, it usually means he has genuinely thought through what is redistributable and what is not — and that he is confident the kitchen can absorb the change without degrading output. Two to three weeks of modified duty is handleable if you protect it deliberately — meaning you hold the cover count where it is, you do not add menu complexity, and you make sure the physical task redistribution Marco described actually happens consistently rather than drifting informally and silently putting load back on Nakajima as the weeks go on. Now — there is a third issue I want to name, because I think this moment is exactly the right time to address it. Have you been thinking about back-of-house support beyond the chef and sous chef level? There is a category of kitchen labor that gets deferred in early restaurant planning and then surfaces as a real operational constraint in week two or three, often at exactly the moment when other pressures are already high.

That is exactly where I was heading next, because it connects to something Marco has mentioned more than once already. The dishwashing situation is adding to the kitchen team's workload. Right now the staff are rotating dish duty during service when someone has a moment, and then everyone pitches in after service to break down. On a lighter night it is manageable. On a full service it creates real bottlenecks. I have seen moments where Marco or Nakajima are waiting at the pass for a clean pan and the person who is supposed to be washing is also trying to finish a plate. I have been thinking about hiring a dishwasher as a dedicated role even before this week's problems arose. Now that Nakajima is at reduced capacity and cannot take on the physical lifting involved in running the dish station, the argument for it feels even stronger.

You are absolutely right to be thinking about this, and the fact that Marco has raised it independently — not because you prompted him, not in the context of a crisis, but as an unsolicited operational observation during normal early running — is one of the strongest signals you can get. Head chefs do not typically raise staffing requests unless they are genuinely seeing friction. The dishwasher role is systematically undervalued in small restaurant planning because the labor cost is visible on the payroll and the benefit is difficult to quantify in advance, but the operational reality is that clean equipment during service is an enabling function — it is what allows everything else to move. When a cook is waiting for a clean pan at 7:45 on a full night, that is not merely a dishwashing problem. The wait propagates forward: the pan comes late, the sauce is delayed, the plate is delayed, the ticket time stretches, and the table that ordered at 7:30 is still waiting at 8:05. Multiply that sequence across several tables over the course of a full service and you have a meaningfully different guest experience than the one you designed. The argument for a dedicated dishwasher is always strong in a kitchen like yours, and it is especially strong right now given that Nakajima's back situation means the heavy lifting and physical rotation involved in running the dish station — exactly the kind of task that drifts toward whoever is available — is explicitly not available to him for the next few weeks. Have you identified any candidates, or are you starting from scratch on this search as well?

I actually have one lead already, which is part of why I feel slightly less panicked about the dishwasher piece than about the server replacement. There is a woman named Mrs. Yoneda who lives in the same building as the restaurant — we're at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu and she has a unit on one of the upper floors. She is 58 years old, and from what I understand she has had some kitchen work experience in the past, though not in a restaurant setting specifically. I've only had a brief, informal conversation with her so far. She knows the building, she is extremely close — the commute is essentially zero — and she seemed genuinely open to the idea when I mentioned it in passing about a week ago. I have not had a formal conversation with her yet. On the server side: I have already moved on that one. A woman named Sara Komatsu, age 23, started November 17. She was referred by Yui — they know each other from a previous job. She came in for a working trial on Sunday and I thought she handled herself well enough for someone brand new to this context. She has no specific experience with Italian restaurant service but she is trained, she is quick on her feet, and she was attentive to the feedback Eiko gave her during the trial shift.

Good — you have already acted on the most urgent item, and that was exactly the right call. Sitting on the server vacancy even another week would have cost you more in service strain than the cost of a quick hire. Let me give you my honest read on each. On Sara Komatsu: she started November 17, which means as of today she has been with you for two days. You are running her in live service during a period when the team is already under stress, the floor is already short, and there is no buffer to catch her mistakes. That is a real sink-or-swim situation, and it can go either way depending on the person. The single thing that makes this hire feel more solid than a cold hire off a job board is the Yui referral. A peer referral in a small service team tends to produce someone who already has an informal understanding of the culture and expectations, because Yui will have described the restaurant to her in more candid terms than any job posting could capture — the pace, the way Marco runs his pass, what Eiko values in a floor team member, what kind of guests come in. Yui also has a professional stake in the referral working well, because her own standing in the team is attached to it. That social dynamic means she is more likely to actively support Sara's integration rather than leaving her to navigate alone. My strong recommendation is to ask Eiko to invest specific, deliberate attention in Sara this week — not just the physical layout and the menu structure, but the rhythm of the pass, the way Marco and the kitchen communicate during a busy ticket run, the unwritten rules about how tables are approached and how quickly guests expect acknowledgment at Osteria Morishita specifically. Whatever early patterns have already emerged from your first two weeks of regulars — those things will not be documented anywhere, but they are often exactly what separates service that merely functions from service that feels like it belongs to this room. I would also suggest you or Eiko check in with Sara at the end of each shift this week, even just for five minutes. Not to evaluate her, but to give her a channel to ask questions she might otherwise sit on. New staff in stressful environments often hesitate to ask basic questions because they do not want to seem unprepared, and that silence can compound into avoidable errors. What is Sara's availability like — is she part-time like Naoki was, or does she have more flexibility? On Mrs. Yoneda as dishwasher candidate: the proximity is a genuine operational advantage that should not be treated as a minor detail, and I want to be clear about why. When a kitchen support staff member calls in sick at 5:30 on a Thursday evening, the difference between someone who can be at your station in three minutes and someone with a forty-five-minute commute is the difference between a solved problem and a scramble where Marco is doing dishes and cooking at the same time. At 58 years old with prior kitchen experience, she is also likely to bring the kind of steady, focused stamina and physical discipline that comes from having done real work over a long period — which is often a more reliable indicator of on-the-job performance than youth or prior restaurant-specific experience. What is holding you back from moving the conversation with her from informal to formal?

My hesitation about Mrs. Yoneda is partly the time pressure of everything else this week — I have been running from one thing to the next and there has not been a quiet moment. But it is also partly that I want to have a clear offer ready before I sit down with her. I do not want to propose something vague and then have the terms shift on her two weeks in. I want to think through the hours, the compensation, the scope of the role. On Sara: she is part-time, similar in structure to how Naoki was set up, but she told me she can commit to four nights a week, which is more availability than Naoki had toward the end of his time with us. That extra availability matters because I have been thinking about adding a Saturday lunch service sometime in December, and I would need floor coverage for that. But honestly the December lunch expansion feels like a secondary concern right now. What I really want is to stabilize what we already have. We are two weeks old. I want to get through the next two to three weeks without something else going wrong. My question for you is: with the current setup — Sara in her first days, Mrs. Yoneda potentially coming on for dishes but not yet formalized, and Nakajima at reduced hours — is the buffer enough, or are there gaps I am not seeing clearly because I am too close to it?

And one more thing on Nakajima before you answer that — he said two to three weeks but that is his own estimate, made without seeing anyone. He mentioned physio in passing as something he might look into, but as far as I know he has not actually seen a doctor yet. Should I be pushing him to get a proper medical assessment and give me a clearer timeline? I want to be supportive because I know back issues can be sensitive, and Nakajima has been excellent — losing him even partially right now is a real blow. But I also need to plan honestly and I cannot anchor next month's kitchen schedule to a self-diagnosis.

Let me take the Nakajima question first, because it is the right question to ask and the answer directly shapes how confidently you can plan everything else. Yes — you should ask Nakajima to see a physician this week and to come back to you and Marco with a timeline grounded in a medical opinion rather than intuition. Frame it explicitly as concern for his wellbeing rather than as operational pressure, and that framing will be accurate: back pain that goes unexamined and is simply waited out can turn a minor muscle issue into a significantly longer problem if the underlying cause is not identified. His two-to-three-week estimate, offered without a medical opinion, is an optimistic guess — and it may well be correct, but you should not be building your operational plan for the coming month around an unexamined guess. A physician assessment this week gives you one of two outcomes, both of which are better than the current uncertainty. If it confirms a straightforward strain with a clear return-to-full-capacity timeline, you can plan with confidence. If it reveals something more complex — a disc issue, something requiring physiotherapy over a longer period — you need to know that now, not in week four when you discover that Nakajima will not be back at full capacity in December. You are not being unsupportive by asking him to get it looked at properly. You are being a responsible employer, and you are also signaling that you want him to take his own condition seriously enough to address it rather than push through it. Most people receive that well when it is framed correctly. Now, your broader question about whether the current buffer is sufficient. My honest assessment: it is enough for the next two to three weeks if nothing else changes, but the margin is thin and there is no slack in the system. Sara Komatsu started November 17 and is in her first days of learning the room and the rhythm of service. Nakajima is on modified duty with an unconfirmed medical timeline. Mrs. Yoneda is a strong candidate for the dishwasher role but has not yet been formally engaged, which means that role remains essentially unfilled. If any single one of those three situations moves in the wrong direction — Sara has a family emergency and misses several shifts, Mrs. Yoneda decides after your formal conversation that the hours or the compensation do not work for her, or Nakajima's condition turns out to be more serious than a muscle strain — you will feel it immediately and with nothing to absorb it. There are two things I would push you to treat as genuinely urgent rather than as items to get to once things calm down. First: have the formal conversation with Mrs. Yoneda in the next 48 hours. The hesitation about defining the role clearly is valid preparation, not a reason to delay the conversation. Think through the hours now — likely the dinner service window plus approximately one hour before service for setup and one hour after for breakdown and full clean, four to five nights per week. Think through a fair compensation rate for kitchen support work in central Tokyo, which will likely fall in the range of 1,150 to 1,350 yen per hour depending on your read of her experience and the demands of the role. Set a probationary period — four weeks is standard — so that both of you have a defined point to assess how it is working. The clarity you bring to that conversation is a gesture of respect to her, not just a logistical protection for yourself. Second: on the December Saturday lunch question, I would encourage you to set a formal decision gate rather than leaving it as an open question that creates low-grade pressure. Pick a date — December 5th is reasonable — and define exactly what the conditions need to look like before you add a service format. Something like: Sara is integrated and operating confidently without close supervision, Nakajima is back to full hours and cleared by a physician, and the dishwasher role is filled and past the first week of live service. If all three are true by December 5th, you add the Saturday lunch. If any of them is unresolved, you delay to January and protect the quality of what you are already delivering. The restaurant that is two weeks old and already expanding is almost always making a mistake, and your instinct to stabilize first is exactly right. Hold that instinct.
